web.title: List of most expensive films
web.description:
It is not clear which film is the most expensive ever made, due to the secretive nature of [Hollywood accounting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_accounting). _[Star Wars: The Force Awakens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Wars:_The_Force_Awakens)_ holds the official record with a net [budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_budgeting) of $536 million. The production of the third and fourth _[Avengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Marvel_Cinematic_Universe_films)_ films— _[Infinity War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avengers:_Infinity_War)_ and _[Endgame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avengers:_Endgame)_—stands as the most expensive [back-to-back film production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back-to-back_film_production), with a cost of over $1 billion. The 1990s saw two thresholds crossed: 1994's _[True Lies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/True_Lies)_ cost $100 million and 1997's _[Titanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanic_(1997_film))_ cost $200 million, both directed by [James Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cameron). ## Most expensive productions (unadjusted for inflation) | Rank | Title | Year | Cost (est.)

Record-holders [[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Finler_(2003)-285) It is not known for certain which was the first film to cost $1million or more to produce, and several myths have grown over time: [D. W. Griffith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D._W._Griffith)'s _[Intolerance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intolerance_(film))_ (1916) was reputed to have cost $2 million, but accounts show that it only cost $385,906.77;[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-286) additionally, _[A Daughter of the Gods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Daughter_of_the_Gods)_ (1916) was advertised as costing a million dollars, but _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_(magazine))_ estimated its true cost at $850,000. [[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Hall_&_Neale_(2010)-206) The first film that is confirmed to have had a $1million budget is _[Foolish Wives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foolish_Wives)_ (1922), with the studio advertising it as "The First Real Million Dollar Picture". The most expensive film of the silent era was _[Ben-Hur: A Tale of the Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben-Hur:_A_Tale_of_the_Christ_(1925_film))_ (1925),[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Hall_&_Neale_(2010)-206) costing about $4 million—twenty-five times the $160,000 average cost of an MGM feature. [[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Finler_(2003)-285) It is unclear which [sound-era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_film) production superseded it as the most expensive film, although this is commonly attributed to _[Hell's Angels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell's_Angels_(film))_ (1930), directed by [Howard Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Hughes); the accounts for _Hell's Angels_ show it cost $2.8 million, but Hughes publicised it as costing $4 million, selling it to the media as the most expensive film ever made. [[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Eyman_(1997)-287) The first film to seriously challenge the record was _[Gone with the Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gone_with_the_Wind_(film))_, reported to have cost about $3.9–4.25 million,[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Hall_&_Neale_(2010)-206) although sources from the time state that _Ben-Hur_ and—erroneously— _Hell's Angels_ cost more. | Year | Production | Cost (est.)

[↑](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_ref-war_and_peace_161-0)The $100 million figure, based on Soviet statements, appeared frequently in the U.S. press in 1968, when _War and Peace_ was released in the country. _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times)_ reported it was "the most expensive film ever made... Yet, the protocols of the Soviet [State Committee for Cinematography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Committee_for_Cinematography) from 25 August 1964 record a meeting of the agency's directors in which a final budget of 8.5 million [Soviet ruble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_ruble) was approved for the series; it included all expenses to be made, including 2.51 million to cover those of the Soviet Ministry of Defense, which supplied thousands of soldiers as extras and other assistance.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-151) According to the producers' financial statements, compiled after the work on the series was completed in August 1967, the total cost of the film came to 8,291,712 Soviet ruble[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-FR-152)—or $9,213,013 with the 1967 0.9 ruble = $1 exchange rate.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-CBR-153) It is technically impossible to adjust the ruble for inflation since the Soviet Union did not formally acknowledge it; instead, the USSR would periodically reprice everything from goods to labour to services. Inflation is usually measured in Western [free market economies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism) using a [price index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price_index) such as the [consumer price index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_price_index), but no such measure existed in the case of the Soviet Union. However, it is possible to measure the increase in average annual earnings in the Soviet Union and there is typically a strong correlation between average earnings and inflation.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-MeasuringWorth-154) In 1965 the average annual wage in the Soviet Union was 1,158 Soviet rubles,[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Klachko_(1988)-155) and in October 2021 the average monthly salary in Russia was 54,649 [Russian rubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_ruble) (the Russian ruble replaced the Soviet ruble in Russia after the fall of the Soviet Union), amounting to approximately 655,788 rubles per year.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Rosstat_(2021-10)-156) This puts salary inflation at over 57,000% (if the [1998 redenomination of the ruble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_ruble#Seventh_ruble,_1_January_1998_%E2%80%93) is factored in, but if not then the true inflation level is 1,000 times higher at 57,000,000%). Applying this rate of inflation to the original cost (8,291,712 rubles) of _War and Peace_ would yield an approximate amount of 4.7 billion Russian rubles. At an exchange rate of approximately 74 rubles to the US dollar,[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Inland_Revenue-157) this would be equivalent to about US$64 million in 2021, and considerably less than the $700 million figure that is often reported.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-King_(2008)-158)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Wilner_(2008)-159)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Kehr_(2007)-160) 50. As part of the [Marshall Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Plan) following [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II), the [Deutsche Mark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Mark) replaced the Reichsmark in 1948 to stave off [hyperinflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation). However, this was not a simple [redenomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redenomination) exercise: while the Deutsche Mark replaced the Reichsmark at an official rate of DM 1 to RM 10, this only applied to the actual currency, with wages, products and services charged at a rate of DM 1 to RM 1 (see [Deutsche Mark: Currency reform of June 1948](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Mark#Currency_reform_of_June_1948)). This was equivalent to introducing 1000% inflation into the old currency before replacing it. As of 1948, _Metropolis_ would have cost RM 6.2 million adjusted for inflation according to the German [consumer price index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_price_index); redenomination would have inflated that to RM 62 million, which would have been equivalent to DM 6.2 million in the new currency.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-inflation-DE-165) This only applied to [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany), but following [German reunification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_reunification), the Deutsche Mark later replaced the [East German mark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_German_mark) and exchanged at parity. The second redenomination occurred in 1999 when Germany converted to the [euro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro), and this time fully adhered to the conventions of a basic redenomination, with all financial assets exchanged at a rate of DM 1.95583 to €1;[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-166) at this time, _Metropolis_ would have cost DM 29 million,[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-inflation-DE-165) equivalent to €15 million after conversion. At 2021 prices, it would cost about €20 million,[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-inflation-DE-165) equivalent to US$24 million at an exchange rate of €0.846 to the dollar.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Inland_Revenue-157) Often reported as having cost $200 million at the value of modern money,[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Total_Sci-Fi_Online_(2007,_Time_Tunnel:_Metropolis)-167)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Rotten_Tomatoes_(2007,_Metropolis_(1927))-168) this estimate is clearly in error by a factor of ten; it is most likely that it came about by adjusting the original cost for inflation, converting the German marks to euros, and then converting the euro figure to US dollars. The process probably failed to account for the fact that the original cost was in Reichsmarks and not Deutsche Marks, so must be divided by 10 to get the equivalent Deutsche Mark value.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films#cite_note-Marcuse_(2005)-169) In applying this methodology, the estimate would come down to about $20 million, and more in line with the CPI figure. 51. [Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twentieth_Century_Fox) claimed the film had cost in total $44 million, of which $31,115,000 represented the direct negative cost and the rest distribution, print and advertising expenses.
